## Discriminatory strategies

<br>

```{r}
#| label: discrim-types
#| include: false

discrim <- tribble(
  ~Strategy, ~Label, ~Definition,
  "Parity", "P", "Equal division between ingroup and outgroup",
  "Maximum joint profit", "MJP", "Maximise points to the others in total",
  "Maximum ingroup profit", "MIP", "Maximise points to ingroup members in absolute terms",
  "Maximum differentiation", "MD", "Maximise the ingroup > outgroup difference",
  "Favouritism", "FAV", "Combination of MD and MIP"
)
discrim
```

```{r}
#| label: discrim-tab

discrim |> 
  gt() |> 
  tab_options(
    table.width = pct(100),
    table.font.size = px(26),
    column_labels.font.weight = "bold"
  ) |>
    opt_stylize()
```

## Tajfel's matrices 

```{r}
#| label: matrix-example
#| include: false

matrix <- tibble(
  Response = LETTERS[1:13],
  "...member 8 of the **overestimators** group" = seq(19,7),
  "...member 27 of the **underestimators** group" = seq(1,25, 2)
) |>
  pivot_longer(-Response, 
               names_to = "Person", 
               values_to = "value") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = Response, 
              values_from = value)
matrix
```

```{r}
#| label: matrix-tab

matrix |> 
  gt() |>
  fmt_markdown(columns = everything()) |> 
  cols_width(
    Person ~ pct(30)  # Make first column narrower
  ) |> 
  tab_options(
    table.width = pct(100),
    table.font.size = px(26),
    column_labels.font.weight = "bold"
  ) |>
  opt_stylize()
```

::: {.incremental .text-small}
- You always assign values to other people (not yourself).
- Select one option (A-M), which corresponds to two values. In this example:
  - M = Maximum joint profit (MJP).
  - A = Ingroup favourtism (for overestimators) (FAV).
  
:::

::: {.citation-footer}
[@bourhis1994]
:::

## Tajfel's matrices 

```{r}
#| label: matrix-tab-repeat

matrix |> 
  gt() |>
  fmt_markdown(columns = everything()) |> 
  cols_width(
    Person ~ pct(30)  # Make first column narrower
  ) |> 
  tab_options(
    table.width = pct(100),
    table.font.size = px(26),
    column_labels.font.weight = "bold"
  ) |>
  opt_stylize()
```

::: {.incremental .text-small}

- This example matrix measures the "pull" of **FAV** on **MJP**.
  - e.g., selecting **A** would count as a "pull" of 12 positions from **M**.
- That value is contrasted to responses on a comparison/control matrix.
- This results in possible values from -12 to +12.

:::

::: {.citation-footer}
[@bourhis1994]
:::

## Pull scores

```{r}
#| label: pull-score-examples
#| include: false

pull_examples <- tribble(
  ~Discrimination, ~Pull, ~Intensity,
  "Outgroup", 4, "Low",
  "Outgroup", 8, "Medium", 
  "Outgroup", 12, "High",
  "None", 0, "None",
  "Ingroup", -4, "Low",
  "Ingroup", -8, "Medium",
  "Ingroup", -12, "High"
) |>
  mutate(
    Discrimination = factor(Discrimination,
                           levels = c("Outgroup", "None", "Ingroup")),
    Intensity = factor(Intensity,
                      levels = c("High", "Medium", "Low", "None"))
  )
pull_examples
```

```{r}
#| label: pull-examples-plot
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-align: center

pull_examples |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = "", y = Pull, 
             color = Discrimination, alpha = Intensity)) +
  geom_point(size = 6) +
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Dark2", name = "Discrimination") +
  scale_alpha_manual(values = c("High" = 1.0, "Medium" = 0.7, "Low" = 0.4, "None" = 1.0),
                     guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-13, 13), breaks = seq(-12, 12, 4)) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(),
        axis.title.x = element_blank(),
        axis.ticks.x = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.minor.x = element_blank(),
        legend.position = c(1.1, 0.53),
        legend.justification = c(0, 0.5),
        legend.key.height = unit(1.2, "cm"),
        plot.margin = margin(5, 60, 5, 5, "mm")) +
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off")
```

## Significance of the work

<br>

- Ingroup benefit and outgroup punishment was evident, even in arbitrary or "minimal" conditions.

::: {.fragment}
- Meaningful social categories, such as race, gender, age etc., are not required to discriminate against others.
:::

::: {.fragment}
- It formed a foundation of Social Identity Theory [@tajfel1979integrative].
:::

## Groups and social identity theory

> ... explicit references to group membership are logically necessary for operationalizing in these minimal situations the major independent variable—that is, social categorization per se. This requires not merely that the subjects perceive themselves as similar to or different from others as *individuals*, but that they are members of discrete and discontinuous categories—that is, "groups".

[@tajfel1979integrative [p. 39]] [*emphasis in the original*]

Citation count: 41,343

##  Groups and social identity theory

<br>

>It was as if that, just by inserting the word ‘group’ into the experimental instructions, the s’s definition of the situation was radically altered.

<br>

[@billig1973 [p. 48]]

Citation count: 2,538

## Conflict signals

- Why might a feature similarity or difference between individuals matter?

::: {.fragment}
- Cognitive neuroscience research shows that conflict in general is an aversive stimulus that guides behaviour.

## Combined results

<br>

- Qualitatively similar minimal group paradigm effects are obtained ***without group assignment***.

::: {.fragment}
- Conflict tasks show that **43.1 % more money** (in relative terms) is given to individuals based on arbitrary sameness versus difference outcomes, ***in the absence of group assignment***.
:::

## Conclusion

- Is group division required to treat people differently? 

  - **No**
  
- Sameness versus difference ***between individuals*** is important to consider theoretically and empirically.

::: {.callout-important .fragment}
## Constraints on generality
We are ***not*** claiming that group division and social identity are unimportant or that differences between individuals can tell the whole story.
:::

## Implications

  - **Empirical:** When studying group bias and discrimination, sameness vs difference between individuals needs separating from the effect of group-based manipulations.
  
::: {.fragment}
  - **Theoretical:** Core tenets of Social Identity Theory need revision:
  
      - Other cognitive and neural mechanisms are likely to be at play in social contexts, such as the affective consequences of domain-general conflict detection and resolution.
      
:::

## Criticism

  >Ok, fine, but groups are "perceived" or "implicitly construed", even when groups a never mentioned.

::: {.fragment}
Three things are relevant here:
::: 

::: {.fragment .text-small}
1. Such an interpretation is in direct opposition to the explicit claims made in Social Identity Theory [-@tajfel1979integrative]. 
:::

::: {.fragment .text-small}
2. It is more difficult to conceptualise conflict tasks in terms of implicit groups. e.g., to consider trial-by-trial (in)congruence as outgroup vs ingroup processing. 
:::

::: {.fragment .text-small}
3. Social conflict tasks (like the ones used here) have been used for decades without the results being attributed to group-based or identity processes.
:::

## EHA: How and why is it useful?

- You can ask questions about "temporal states" of cognition
  - e.g., When does a psychological state start and finish? How does it evolve with increased waiting time? Is it time-locked to other events?

::: {.fragment}
- Theory
- Psychophysiology
- Individual differences
:::

::: {.citation-footer}
[@panis2024]
:::

## EHA: A tutorial

- We have written a tutorial paper aimed at those interested in cognition and cognitive neuroscience. It covers:

  - Data wrangling.
  - Multi-level regression modelling (Bayesian & frequentist).
  - Inference.
  - Planning via data simulation. 

- All of the materials and tutorials are available on [GitHub](https://github.com/sven-panis/Tutorial_Event_History_Analysis).

::: {.citation-footer}
[@panis2024]

## Mapping psychological constructs

- Model parameters map onto latent psychological constructs.

```{r}
#| label: lba-params
#| include: false

lba_params <- tribble(
  ~Parameter, ~Label, ~Construct,
  "Start point", "A", "response bias",
  "Drift rate", "v", "signal-to-noise ratio",
  "Threshold", "b", "response caution",
  "Non-decision time", "t<sub>0</sub>", "stimulus encoding and motor response"
)
lba_params
```

```{r}
#| label: lba-params-table

lba_params |> 
  gt() |> 
  fmt_markdown(columns = everything()) |> 
  tab_options(
    table.width = pct(80),
    table.font.size = px(26),
    column_labels.font.weight = "bold"
  ) |> 
  opt_stylize()
```
